# World_geography claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 707 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 860 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (860 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/world_geography.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

- **Source:** `source.aap_katabatic_winds`
- **URL:** https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/ice-and-atmosphere/atmosphere/winds-waves-and-temperatures/from-the-katabatic-to-the-polar-vortex/

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.katabatic_winds`: unverified

> **Claim:** Katabatic winds form when air over Antarctica's ice cools, becomes heavier and flows downhill toward the coast.

- **Concept:** Antarctica's extremes (`concept.world_geography.antarctica_extremes`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L88 “Antarctica” · `card.world_geography.088.c4` (text): Dry as a desert, windy as an open freezer / A desert is defined by how little precipitation falls, usually less than about 250 to 500 mm a year, not by heat. Antarctica's snowfall adds up to only about 150 mm of rain a year, so it's a cold, dry desert. And the wind? Air over the ice cools, gets heavier and pours downhill toward the coast. These katabatic winds are like the cold air spilling out of an open freezer, only continent-sized.
- **Tested by:**
  - L88 `question.world_geography.088.q2`: How can an ice-covered continent be a desert? → **Very little snow falls there each year**
  - L90 `question.world_geography.090.q3`: Level 81 called Australia the driest continent except one. Which one is drier? → **Antarctica, where snowfall equals very little rain**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Australian Antarctic Program: 'The air close to the icy surface cools ... This makes it heavier and forces it to flow downhill'; the flow down to the coast makes the katabatic. Wikipedia's katabatic wind article: dense cold air built up over Antarctica's elevated ice sheets blows out downslope toward the coast. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katabatic_wind
- **Weak evidence:** one-page, weak-pages (revisit first)

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.world_geography.katabatic_winds source.aap_katabatic_winds --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.tokyo_topped_earlier`: unverified

> **Claim:** Tokyo was the world's largest city in earlier UN rankings; the UN's 2025 ranking, made with a new method, put Jakarta first.

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.cyclone_not_at_equator`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator, so tropical cyclones form some distance away from it.

- **Concept:** How tropical cyclones work (`concept.world_geography.tropical_cyclones`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L36 “Hurricanes and Typhoons” · `card.world_geography.036.c3` (text): The spin comes from Earth / Here's Level 33's Coriolis effect again. It makes these storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. But the Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator, so a storm there has nothing to get it spinning. That's why tropical cyclones form some distance away from the Equator, even though the water there is plenty warm.
- **Tested by:**
  - L36 `question.world_geography.036.q3`: Using Level 33: why don't tropical cyclones form right on the Equator? → **The Coriolis effect is zero there**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Newsweek quoting NOAA and UMass Lowell scientists: the Coriolis effect is essentially zero at the equator, so there is not enough background spin to organize tropical cyclones there. Sources: https://www.newsweek.com/hurricane-crossing-equator-weather-physics-1790522
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not. / Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S
  - L32 “Why the Equator Is Hot” · `card.world_geography.032.c3` (fact): Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. / That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere, so distance can't be what makes summer hot.   - L77 “The Caribbean” · `card.world_geography.077.c3` (text): Hurricane fuel / A hurricane is a rotating storm that forms over tropical or subtropical waters, and its fuel is warm ocean water: at least 26.5°C. ### ☐ `fact.world_geography.earth_tilt_23_5`: unverified

> **Claim:** Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, which is why the tropics lie about 23.5° from the Equator and the polar circles about 23.5° from the poles.

- **Concept:** The tropics (`concept.world_geography.tropics`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “The Equator and the Tropics” · `card.world_geography.004.c3` (text): The tropics: where the Sun turns around / Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so the spot where the noon Sun stands directly overhead drifts north and south through the year. It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not. / Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S
  - L4 “The Equator and the Tropics” · `card.world_geography.004.c4` (text): The polar circles: days that last all day / Now go about 23.5° from each pole: that same tilt again. You reach the Arctic Circle at about 66.5° N and the Antarctic Circle at about 66.5° S. On these lines the Sun stays up for a full day at least once a year, and stays down for a full day, too. Keep going toward a pole and it stretches to six months. Try explaining bedtime there in June.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Oceania and the Poles” · `card.world_geography.090.c4` (text): Taking turns with the Sun / Because Earth's axis is tilted, the two poles share the daylight by taking turns. For six months of the year the Sun never rises over one pole and never sets over the other. Then they swap. Level 4's tilt, pushed to its extreme: one pole's endless summer day is the other pole's endless winter night.
- **Tested by:**
  - L4 `question.world_geography.004.q2`: Why do the tropics lie about 23.5° north and south of the Equator? → **Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°**

  - L38 `question.world_geography.038.q3`: From Level 4: the Greeks' torrid zone lay between which two lines? → **The Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn**
  - L42 `question.world_geography.042.q3`: From Level 4: between which two lines do tropical rainforests mainly grow? → **The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn**

  - L71 `question.world_geography.071.q3`: From Level 4: most of North America lies between which two lines? → **The Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer**
  - L77 `question.world_geography.077.q3`: Hurricanes form over tropical waters. From Level 4, what sets the tropics apart from everywhere else? → **Only there can the Sun stand directly overhead**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: Earth's inclination of about 23 1/2 degrees sets the Arctic Circle; the tropics mark the Sun's greatest declination. The Arctic Circle equals 90 degrees minus the axial tilt. Sources: https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/skytellers/seasons/

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.everest_limestone`: unverified

> **Claim:** The rock at Everest's summit is limestone that formed on an ancient sea floor, and it holds fossils of sea creatures.

- **Concept:** Everest's sea-floor summit (`concept.world_geography.everest_sea_floor`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L17 “How Mountains Rise” · `card.world_geography.017.c1` (text): There are fossil sea creatures at the top of Mount Everest. / The highest rock on the planet, about 8,849 m above sea level, formed at the bottom of a sea. Something lifted it higher than anything else on Earth.
  - L17 “How Mountains Rise” · `card.world_geography.017.c4` (fact): The Himalayas are still rising. / India is still pushing into Asia, so the job isn't finished. That same push is how an old sea floor ended up on the roof of the world: the collision thrust fossil-packed limestone all the way to Everest's summit. Level 7 measured heights from sea level. Everest's top rock started out below it.
  - L18 “The Rock Cycle” · `card.world_geography.018.c3` (text): Sedimentary: built in layers / Weathering breaks rock into pieces and erosion carries them off. Those bits, plus the remains of living things, settle in layers, and the lowest get pressed into solid rock: sedimentary rock. Limestone is often built from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. That's what Level 17's Everest summit is made of.
- **Tested by:**
  - L17 `question.world_geography.017.q2`: Why are there fossils of sea creatures at the top of Mount Everest? → **Sea-floor limestone was thrust up by the collision**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. IUGS: summit rocks are Ordovician limestones from a shallow sea containing marine fossils. Britannica: the limestone atop Everest was ocean floor with many marine fossils. Montana State's Everest project agrees. Sources: https://www.montana.edu/everest/facts/summit-limestone.html

And it stands only about 3° south of the Equator, deep in the tropics, which is exactly why snow up there sounded so ridiculous in 1848.

Those lines are meridians, and they measure longitude: how far east or west you are, from 0° up to 180°. Unlike parallels, meridians all meet at the poles. But which slice is zero? ### ☐ `fact.world_geography.earth_turns_15_per_hour`: unverified

> **Claim:** Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, which is 15° of longitude every hour.

That worked fine until railways spread, and a timetable had to juggle a different local time at every stop.
  - L5 “Time Zones” · `card.world_geography.005.c3` (text): Twenty-four slices of time / The fix was standard time. Cut the globe into 24 zones along meridians 15° apart, counted from Greenwich, and make each zone one hour apart. The system was adopted at the same 1884 conference that picked the prime meridian.   - L10 “Checkpoint: Reading the Planet” · `card.world_geography.010.c4` (text): Opposite in time, too / Your antipode is 180° of longitude away, and Earth turns 15° an hour, so it's about 12 hours off from you.   - L64 “Russia, the Biggest Country” · `card.world_geography.064.c4` (text): Eleven clocks, one country / All that width shows up on the clock. Russia spans 11 time zones, from Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea to Kamchatka on the Pacific. Remember Level 5: Earth turns 15° of longitude every hour, so each zone covers a slice of about that width. Kaliningrad and Kamchatka are 10 hours apart. When it's 9:00 a.m. in Kaliningrad, it's 7:00 p.m. in Kamchatka. Breakfast at one end, dinner at the other. / 11 time zones · 10 hours from end to end

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.earth_tilt_23_5`: unverified

> **Claim:** Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, which is why the tropics lie about 23.5° from the Equator and the polar circles about 23.5° from the poles.

- **Concept:** The tropics (`concept.world_geography.tropics`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “The Equator and the Tropics” · `card.world_geography.004.c3` (text): The tropics: where the Sun turns around / Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so the spot where the noon Sun stands directly overhead drifts north and south through the year. It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not. / Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S
  - L4 “The Equator and the Tropics” · `card.world_geography.004.c4` (text): The polar circles: days that last all day / Now go about 23.5° from each pole: that same tilt again. You reach the Arctic Circle at about 66.5° N and the Antarctic Circle at about 66.5° S. On these lines the Sun stays up for a full day at least once a year, and stays down for a full day, too. Keep going toward a pole and it stretches to six months. Try explaining bedtime there in June.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Oceania and the Poles” · `card.world_geography.090.c4` (text): Taking turns with the Sun / Because Earth's axis is tilted, the two poles share the daylight by taking turns. For six months of the year the Sun never rises over one pole and never sets over the other. Then they swap. Level 4's tilt, pushed to its extreme: one pole's endless summer day is the other pole's endless winter night.
- **Tested by:**
  - L4 `question.world_geography.004.q2`: Why do the tropics lie about 23.5° north and south of the Equator? → **Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°**
  - L32 `question.world_geography.032.q3`: Using Level 4's tropics: which town collects the most solar energy over a year? → **A town on the Equator**
  - L38 `question.world_geography.038.q3`: From Level 4: the Greeks' torrid zone lay between which two lines? → **The Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn**
  - L42 `question.world_geography.042.q3`: From Level 4: between which two lines do tropical rainforests mainly grow? → **The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn**
  - L51 `question.world_geography.051.q3`: From Level 4: which set of lines crosses Africa and no other continent? → **The Equator and both tropics**
  - L71 `question.world_geography.071.q3`: From Level 4: most of North America lies between which two lines? → **The Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer**
  - L77 `question.world_geography.077.q3`: Hurricanes form over tropical waters. From Level 4, what sets the tropics apart from everywhere else? → **Only there can the Sun stand directly overhead**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: Earth's inclination of about 23 1/2 degrees sets the Arctic Circle; the tropics mark the Sun's greatest declination. The Arctic Circle equals 90 degrees minus the axial tilt. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/place/Arctic-Circle, https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/skytellers/seasons/

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.tundra_no_trees`: unverified

> **Claim:** Trees can't grow on the tundra: the season is too short to grow wood, strong winds dry and batter plants, and permafrost keeps roots from reaching deep enough for support.

- **Concept:** The tundra (`concept.world_geography.tundra_biome`)
- **Appears in:**

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.gps_travel_time`: unverified

> **Claim:** A receiver finds its distance to each satellite from how long the signal took to arrive, since the signal travels at the speed of light.

- **Concept:** How GPS finds you (`concept.world_geography.gps_positioning`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “How Your Phone Knows Where You Are” · `card.world_geography.009.c3` (text): Time becomes distance / Your phone notes when each message arrives. The signal travels at the speed of light, so the delay tells your phone how far away that satellite is. Know how far you are from three satellites, and there's enough information to work out where you are. It's like counting the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge how far away a storm is, only with radio waves and far better clocks.
  - L9 “How Your Phone Knows Where You Are” · `card.world_geography.009.c4` (fact): It takes four satellites, not three. / The satellites' clocks are superb; the one in your phone isn't. At light speed, a tiny timing slip turns into a big miss. So your phone uses a fourth satellite to correct its own clock. The answer comes out as latitude, longitude and altitude: Level 3's two numbers, plus your height.
- **Tested by:**
  - L9 `question.world_geography.009.q1`: How many satellites does a GPS receiver need for a precise fix? → **Four**
  - L9 `question.world_geography.009.q2`: GPS satellites never hear from your phone. So how does it find its distance to one? → **It times how long the signal took to arrive**
  - L9 `question.world_geography.009.q3`: Besides altitude, a GPS fix gives your position as which pair of numbers from Level 3? → **Latitude and longitude**
  - L37 `question.world_geography.037.q3`: Like GPS in Level 9, counting the seconds from a lightning flash to its thunder turns time into what? → **Distance**
  - L100 `question.world_geography.100.q3`: Why does your phone need a fourth GPS satellite, not just three? → **To correct its own less precise clock**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NASA: a receiver determines its position by calculating how long the signals took to reach it. NOAA: distance = signal speed x travel time. Trimble: travel time x speed of light. Sources: https://geospatial.trimble.com/blog/geospatial/en-US/article/gps-101-learn-how-gps-works, https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_geodesy/geo09_gps.html

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.spheres_interact`: unverified

> **Claim:** Earth's systems all interact with one another; for example, rain falling from the atmosphere links the hydrosphere with the geosphere.

- **Concept:** Earth's connected systems (`concept.world_geography.earth_systems`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L50 “Milestone: The Physical World” · `card.world_geography.050.c2` (text): Four spheres, one planet / Scientists split Earth into connected systems. The geosphere is rock, from the crust down to the core. The hydrosphere is water, and Level 1 showed it covers about 71% of the surface. The atmosphere is the envelope of gas around us. The biosphere is all life. Many add a fifth, the cryosphere, for ice. And all of them constantly interact. / Geosphere · Hydrosphere · Atmosphere · Biosphere

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.alps_fold_mountains`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Alps are fold mountains, pushed up where the Adriatic microplate, a fragment of the African plate, is colliding with the Eurasian plate.

- **Appears in:**
  - L62 “The Alps and Europe's Rivers” · `card.world_geography.062.c2` (text): Europe's crumpled edge / The Alps are the centerpiece of Level 61's southern stripe, arcing from the Mediterranean coast near Nice, France, to Vienna, Austria. They're fold mountains: they form where tectonic plates are pushed together and rock crumples upward, like a rug shoved against a wall. Here the pusher is the Adriatic microplate, a fragment of the African plate, driving into Eurasia. The top of the crumple is Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: Europe and Asia” · `card.world_geography.070.c3` (text): Crumple or dive / Along this belt, plates push into Eurasia: a fragment of Africa behind the Alps, India behind the Himalayas. When continents meet like India and Asia, their rock has about the same density, so neither plate can slide under the other and the crust crumples upward. Compare Level 69's Ring of Fire, where one plate dives beneath another and helps make magma. Crumple, and you get fold mountains. Dive, and you get volcanoes.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Alps arose from the collision of the African and Eurasian plates, with the Adriatic plate (part of Africa) playing the key role. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.orographic_rain`: unverified

> **Claim:** Air rising over mountains cools and drops rain and snow on the way up; coming down the far side, it warms and its clouds fade, leaving a dry rain shadow.

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.subduction_magma`: unverified

> **Claim:** At a subduction zone one plate is pushed down beneath another, and the sinking rock helps melt rock into magma, which can rise and erupt.

- **Concept:** Subduction makes volcanoes (`concept.world_geography.subduction_volcanoes`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L69 “Islands of Fire” · `card.world_geography.069.c3` (text): Where one plate dives under another / Along much of the ring, plates meet at subduction zones, where one plate is pushed down beneath another. The sinking rock helps melt rock into magma, which can rise and erupt. Japan shows the recipe at full strength: it sits where four plates meet (the Pacific, Philippine Sea, Eurasian and North American), and its volcanoes formed largely along subduction zones. The planet recycles its floor, with fireworks.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: Europe and Asia” · `card.world_geography.070.c3` (text): Crumple or dive / Along this belt, plates push into Eurasia: a fragment of Africa behind the Alps, India behind the Himalayas. When continents meet like India and Asia, their rock has about the same density, so neither plate can slide under the other and the crust crumples upward. Compare Level 69's Ring of Fire, where one plate dives beneath another and helps make magma. Crumple, and you get fold mountains. Dive, and you get volcanoes.
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.world_geography.069.q2`: Why do subduction zones produce volcanoes? → **A sinking plate helps melt rock into magma**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: oceanic plates subduct under neighboring plates, and subduction produces the magma that drives eruptions. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/place/Ring-of-Fire
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

> **Claim:** The Tropic of Cancer lies at about 23.5° N and the Tropic of Capricorn at about 23.5° S.

It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not. / Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S
  - L42 “Rainforests” · `card.world_geography.042.c3` (text): Summer that never ends / Tropical rainforests grow mainly in the tropics, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn you met in Level 4. Temperatures stay high and rain is plentiful all year, with little change from season to season. No winter shutdown, no dry spell. Plenty of sunlight and moisture are the building blocks for a huge variety of plants and animals, and the rainforest never runs short of either.
  - L43 “Deserts” · `card.world_geography.043.c3` (text): Where the sky is a lid / Many big deserts sit in belts around 30° to 35° north and south of the Equator, just outside the tropics from Level 4. Air flows from high pressure toward low pressure, the way passengers on a crowded bus spread into the empty seats. That flow is wind. The bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind blows.   - L35 “Monsoons” · `card.world_geography.035.c2` (text): Land heats faster than water / Picture a beach in summer: the sand burns your feet while the sea stays cool. Land heats up faster than water, and a whole continent does the same. In summer, low pressure forms over the hot land. You know Level 33's rule: air flows from high pressure to low. So moist air from the cooler ocean pours inland.
- **Tested by:**
  - L33 `question.world_geography.033.q1`: Which way does wind blow? → **From high pressure toward low pressure**
  - L35 `question.world_geography.035.q2`: Why does the summer monsoon blow from the ocean onto the land? → **The land heats faster, creating low pressure**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. UCAR: winds blow away from high pressure and toward low pressure. NOAA JetStream: wind speed increases as the pressure gradient increases. Sources: https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/how-weather-works/highs-and-lows-air-pressure, https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/synoptic/origin-of-wind

## Currents: The Coriolis Effect (NOAA National Ocean Service)

- **Source:** `source.noaa_coriolis`
- **URL:** https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/04currents1.html
- **License:** US_gov_public_domain · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.coriolis_deflection`: unverified

> **Claim:** Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern; this is the Coriolis effect.

- **Concept:** The Coriolis effect (`concept.world_geography.coriolis_effect`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “Wind and Pressure” · `card.world_geography.033.c4` (text): Trade winds, with a twist / That inflowing air never blows straight at the Equator, because Earth spins underneath it. The spin deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. That's the Coriolis effect. It bends the flow into the trade winds: steady easterlies near the Equator, blowing from the east toward the west. Handy, if your ship is heading for the Americas.
  - L36 “Hurricanes and Typhoons” · `card.world_geography.036.c3` (text): The spin comes from Earth / Here's Level 33's Coriolis effect again. It makes these storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. But the Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator, so a storm there has nothing to get it spinning. That's why tropical cyclones form some distance away from the Equator, even though the water there is plenty warm.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Climate and Weather” · `card.world_geography.040.c3` (text): Down near 30 degrees / Around 30° north and south, that dry air sinks and warms up again. Sinking air blocks clouds from forming, just like on Level 34's leeward slopes, so little rain falls and deserts like the Sahara form. Then the air flows back toward the Equator along the ground, bent by the Coriolis effect. That return flow is the trade winds. Loop closed.
- **Tested by:**
  - L36 `question.world_geography.036.q3`: Using Level 33: why don't tropical cyclones form right on the Equator? → **The Coriolis effect is zero there**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA currents tutorial page 2: as air moves away from the Equator the Coriolis effect deflects it to the right (Northern Hemisphere). AOML: Coriolis makes storms turn counterclockwise in the north, clockwise in the south. Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/04currents2.html, https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd-faq/

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.gps_four_satellites`: unverified

> **Claim:** A precise GPS fix needs four satellites: three to find the position and one to correct the error in the receiver's clock.

- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “How Your Phone Knows Where You Are” · `card.world_geography.009.c3` (text): Time becomes distance / Your phone notes when each message arrives. The signal travels at the speed of light, so the delay tells your phone how far away that satellite is. Know how far you are from three satellites, and there's enough information to work out where you are. It's like counting the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge how far away a storm is, only with radio waves and far better clocks.
  - L9 “How Your Phone Knows Where You Are” · `card.world_geography.009.c4` (fact): It takes four satellites, not three. / The satellites' clocks are superb; the one in your phone isn't. At light speed, a tiny timing slip turns into a big miss. So your phone uses a fourth satellite to correct its own clock. The answer comes out as latitude, longitude and altitude: Level 3's two numbers, plus your height.
- **Tested by:**

  - L9 `question.world_geography.009.q3`: Besides altitude, a GPS fix gives your position as which pair of numbers from Level 3? → **Latitude and longitude**
  - L37 `question.world_geography.037.q3`: Like GPS in Level 9, counting the seconds from a lightning flash to its thunder turns time into what? → **Distance**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA: it takes four satellites, three to determine a position and one to adjust for the error in the receiver's clock. FAA and other guides agree. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorange

At the old end sits Kure Atoll: no volcano in sight, just a ring of coral.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA: the archipelago stretches 'from the island of Hawaii in the southeast to Kure Atoll in the northwest.' Papahanaumokuakea: Kure Atoll is at the extreme northwest end and the oldest in the chain. Sources: https://www.papahanaumokuakea.gov/visit/kure.html, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kure_Atoll

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.winter_water_short`: unverified

> **Claim:** In winter, freezing leaves water in short supply, so plants without ways to conserve it would lose water.

- **Concept:** Deciduous forests and autumn (`concept.world_geography.deciduous_forest`)

  - L45 “Forests of the North” · `card.world_geography.045.c2` (text): Winter is a drought / In winter, much of the water is locked up as ice, so it's in short supply, and a plant with no way to save water would dry out. Deciduous trees solve it bluntly. Before winter, a special layer of cells grows where each leaf's stem meets the tree and cuts the leaf loose. Bare branches aren't a sign of giving up. They're a tree battening down the hatches.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Three Rivers Park District and Michigan State University Extension explain that frozen ground makes water unavailable, so trees drop leaves to stop losing water. At the far tips, north and south, you'll find Mediterranean climates. / Rainforest › savanna › desert › Mediterranean, in both directions

The Sahara, across northern Africa, is the largest hot desert, almost the size of the contiguous United States. Big enough to swallow a country, and still only the runner-up.

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.atoll_darwin`: unverified

> **Claim:** Charles Darwin proposed that atolls form when a reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks, until only a ring of reef around a lagoon remains.

- **Concept:** How atolls form (`concept.world_geography.atoll_formation`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L85 “The Pacific Islands” · `card.world_geography.085.c1` (text): Some Pacific islands are volcanoes. Others are rings left by sunken ones. / Two very different kinds of island. Give one of them enough time and it can turn into the other.
  - L85 “The Pacific Islands” · `card.world_geography.085.c4` (text): Darwin's sinking islands / Charles Darwin worked out the missing step. Coral grows as a reef around a volcanic island. The island slowly sinks, but the reef keeps building upward. Finally the island vanishes under the sea, and only the ring of reef is left around a lagoon: an atoll. In the 1950s, scientists drilled into Enewetak Atoll, went through more than 1 km of coral and hit volcanic rock. The volcano had been down there all along. / Volcano, then reef, then a ring with a lagoon
- **Tested by:**
  - L85 `question.world_geography.085.q2`: Why does an atoll have a lagoon in the middle? → **The volcanic island it circled sank beneath the sea**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. USGS: 'As first hypothesized by Charles Darwin ... As a volcanic island subsides ... the growing reef keeps pace ... the ring-shaped reef forms an atoll with a central lagoon.' Royal Society: atolls formed around islands that subsided, leaving only the reef. Sources: https://royalsociety.org/blog/2024/09/boring-old-coral/, https://www.coraldigest.org/reef_structure/darwinstheory/index.html

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.wind_high_to_low`: unverified

> **Claim:** Wind is air flowing from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure; the bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind.

- **Concept:** Air pressure makes wind (`concept.world_geography.pressure_wind`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “Wind and Pressure” · `card.world_geography.033.c2` (text): Air hates a crowd / Air presses on everything, and in some places it presses harder than in others. Air flows from high pressure toward low pressure, the way passengers on a crowded bus spread into the empty seats. That flow is wind. The bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind blows. A gentle breeze means a small difference. A gale means a big one. / Wind blows from high pressure to low pressure.
  - L35 “Monsoons” · `card.world_geography.035.c2` (text): Land heats faster than water / Picture a beach in summer: the sand burns your feet while the sea stays cool. Land heats up faster than water, and a whole continent does the same. In summer, low pressure forms over the hot land. You know Level 33's rule: air flows from high pressure to low. So moist air from the cooler ocean pours inland.
- **Tested by:**
  - L33 `question.world_geography.033.q1`: Which way does wind blow? → **From high pressure toward low pressure**
  - L35 `question.world_geography.035.q2`: Why does the summer monsoon blow from the ocean onto the land? → **The land heats faster, creating low pressure**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. UCAR: winds blow away from high pressure and toward low pressure. NOAA JetStream: wind speed increases as the pressure gradient increases. Sources: https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/how-weather-works/highs-and-lows-air-pressure, https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/synoptic/origin-of-wind

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.atoll_darwin`: unverified

> **Claim:** Charles Darwin proposed that atolls form when a reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks, until only a ring of reef around a lagoon remains.

- **Concept:** How atolls form (`concept.world_geography.atoll_formation`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L85 “The Pacific Islands” · `card.world_geography.085.c1` (text): Some Pacific islands are volcanoes. Others are rings left by sunken ones. / Two very different kinds of island. Give one of them enough time and it can turn into the other.
  - L85 “The Pacific Islands” · `card.world_geography.085.c4` (text): Darwin's sinking islands / Charles Darwin worked out the missing step. Coral grows as a reef around a volcanic island. The island slowly sinks, but the reef keeps building upward. Finally the island vanishes under the sea, and only the ring of reef is left around a lagoon: an atoll. In the 1950s, scientists drilled into Enewetak Atoll, went through more than 1 km of coral and hit volcanic rock. The volcano had been down there all along. / Volcano, then reef, then a ring with a lagoon
- **Tested by:**
  - L85 `question.world_geography.085.q2`: Why does an atoll have a lagoon in the middle? → **The volcanic island it circled sank beneath the sea**
  - L90 `question.world_geography.090.q4`: From Level 85: an atoll began as what? → **A reef around a volcanic island that sank**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. USGS: 'As first hypothesized by Charles Darwin ... As a volcanic island subsides ... the growing reef keeps pace ... the ring-shaped reef forms an atoll with a central lagoon.' Royal Society: atolls formed around islands that subsided, leaving only the reef. ### ☐ `fact.world_geography.cycle_steps`: unverified

> **Claim:** Water evaporates into vapor, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation such as rain or snow, and moves back across and under the land.

- **Concept:** The water cycle (`concept.world_geography.water_cycle`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L21 “The Water Cycle” · `card.world_geography.021.c2` (text): The Sun lifts, gravity drops / The whole loop runs on two engines. Energy from the Sun warms water until it evaporates and rises as invisible vapor. Up high, the vapor condenses into clouds. Then gravity takes over: the water falls as rain or snow and makes its way back across and under the land. The Sun does the heavy lifting. Gravity handles the delivery, free of charge.

  - L21 `question.world_geography.021.q1`: What two things drive the water cycle? → **Energy from the Sun and gravity**
  - L21 `question.world_geography.021.q2`: A water molecule evaporates from the sea today. Where is it most likely to be in about two weeks? → **Back on the ground or in the sea**
  - L25 `question.world_geography.025.q3`: From Level 21: gravity pulls rain back across the land. What decides which river the rain on your street ends up in? → **The watershed you are standing in**
  - L26 `question.world_geography.026.q3`: From Level 21: the Sun's energy evaporates water from a lake with no outlet. What happens to the lake's salt? → **It stays behind in the lake**

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.altitude_cold`: unverified

> **Claim:** Air gets colder with altitude, so Antarctica's high elevation helps make it colder.

  - L88 “Antarctica” · `card.world_geography.088.c3` (fact): The coldest temperature ever measured on Earth: −89.2 °C. / It was recorded at Vostok station in Antarctica on 21 July 1983. Height is part of the reason. Air gets colder the higher you go, and Antarctica sits higher on average than any other continent. Antarctica is cold partly for the same reason mountaintops are.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Oceania and the Poles” · `card.world_geography.090.c3` (fact): In winter, the South Pole is far colder than the North Pole. / Winter averages about −60 °C at the South Pole and about −40 °C at the North Pole. Two reasons, both from this chapter. Antarctica is high, and air gets colder with altitude. And the Arctic's ice floats on an ocean that's usually warmer than the air above it, while Antarctica gets little heat from the sea.

> **Claim:** An antipode keeps the same latitude number in the other hemisphere, and its longitude is 180° away.

### ☐ `fact.world_geography.greek_colonies`: unverified

> **Claim:** Ancient Greek seafarers founded colonies across the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts, from Spain and France to Italy and North Africa.

- **Concept:** The Mediterranean, a sea that connected peoples (`concept.world_geography.mediterranean_sea`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L63 “The Mediterranean” · `card.world_geography.063.c4` (text): A pond, not a wall / For ancient peoples, this sea was a road. Greek seafarers founded colonies all along the coasts, from Spain and France to Italy, North Africa and the Black Sea. Trade usually came first, and many colonies became trading hubs. The Greeks didn't have the water to themselves, either: the Phoenicians and Etruscans founded colonies too. Hence the frogs. Plenty of neighbors, one shared pond.
